name: Skoog subfacial facelift

lead: The Skoog subfacial facelift is a surgical approach described by Tord Skoog in the late 1960s and early 1970s. Instead of pulling skin, it dissects beneath the facial tissue layer and lifts the deeper structures, including the platysma muscle of the neck.
The appearance goal is a firmer jawline, smoother neck and a less tired lower face. Later techniques, notably those based on the SMAS layer, built on or replaced parts of the approach.

paras: It is performed by a plastic surgeon under anaesthesia through incisions around the ear. Recovery takes weeks, and the surgery is typically discussed in the context of facial ageing.

Facelift complications described on Wikipedia include hematoma, the most common, sensory or motor nerve injury, skin necrosis (smoking raises the risk), infection, scarring and hairline or earlobe distortion.

chain: Dissect beneath the facial tissue layer
Lift and suspend deeper layers with the platysma
angle.text: By repositioning deeper tissue rather than only skin, the technique tightens the lower face and neck contour that sagging softens.

lead: The Skoog subfacial facelift belongs to the history of facelift surgery. Wikipedia places Tord Skoog's introduction of subfacial dissection in 1968 to 1974, as a method that suspends the deeper layers instead of relying on skin tension, and it included dissection of the platysma [1].

The aim is appearance: lifting sagging tissue along the jawline and neck. Skoog's work came after the early "cutaneous" era in which surgeons pulled and trimmed skin. The SMAS concept, described by Mitz and Peyronie in 1976, then became the standard approach [1].
In looksmaxxing discussion the procedure is considered part of hard-maxxing, the surgical end of appearance change.

paras: Wikipedia divides facelift history into eras. The cutaneous period (1900 to 1970) pulled skin, and Eugen Holländer reportedly performed the first facelift in Berlin in 1901. Skoog's subfacial approach followed in 1968 to 1974, then the SMAS period, deep plane and subperiosteal methods, and later volumetric approaches [1].

Hematoma is the most common complication. Greater auricular nerve injury is the most common sensory injury and facial nerve injury the most common motor one. Smoking is reported to raise skin necrosis risk 12-fold. Scarring, hair loss at incisions and distortion of the hairline or earlobe can also occur [1].
Satisfaction is reported to be highest when surgery is done at 50 or younger, and results of skin-only lifts last about 5 to 10 years [1].

timeline.event: Eugen Holländer reportedly performs the first facelift in Berlin [1].
Tord Skoog begins introducing subfacial dissection [1].
Mitz and Peyronie describe the SMAS [1].
